claim: The time it takes a sound to travel from source to ear differs between the ears and creates an interaural delay.
source: The time it takes a sound to travel from source to ear differs between the ears and creates an interaural delay.
evidence: This is a statement of established acoustic physics regarding sound propagation and binaural hearing.

claim: Interaural delay varies systematically with spatial direction.
source: It varies systematically with spatial direction and is generally modeled as a pure time delay, independent of frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of spatial hearing and is supported by the acoustical measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Interaural delay is generally modeled as a pure time delay, independent of frequency.
source: It varies systematically with spatial direction and is generally modeled as a pure time delay, independent of frequency.
evidence: This describes the conventional model in the field.

claim: In acoustical recordings, interaural delay varies with frequency at a fine scale.
source: In acoustical recordings, we found that interaural delay varies with frequency at a fine scale.
evidence: This is directly supported by the acoustical measurements presented in Figure 2 and related analyses.

claim: In physiological recordings of midbrain neurons sensitive to interaural delay, preferred delay varies with sound frequency.
source: In physiological recordings of midbrain neurons sensitive to interaural delay, we found that preferred delay also varies with sound frequency.
evidence: This is directly supported by the electrophysiological recordings from IC neurons presented in Figure 1.

claim: Similar observations of frequency-dependent preferred delay were reported earlier but not incorporated in a functional framework.
source: Similar observations reported earlier were not incorporated in a functional framework.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript showing this property has been observed but not functionally interpreted.

claim: The frequency dependence of acoustical and physiological interaural delays are matched in key respects.
source: We find that the frequency dependence of acoustical and physiological interaural delays are matched in key respects.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4 and related statistical comparisons.

claim: Binaural neurons are tuned to acoustical features of ecological environments, rather than to fixed interaural delays.
source: This suggests that binaural neurons are tuned to acoustical features of ecological environments, rather than to fixed interaural delays.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion drawn from the match between acoustical and physiological data.

claim: The tuning of binaural neurons to frequency-dependent ITDs may emerge from neurons detecting coincidences between input fibers that are mistuned in frequency.
source: Using recordings from the nerve and brainstem we show that this tuning may emerge from neurons detecting coincidences between input fibers that are mistuned in frequency.
evidence: This is supported by the coincidence analysis of auditory nerve fibers (Figure 6) and intracellular recordings from MSO (Figure 7).

claim: Interaural time differences (ITDs) are used by many species to localize sounds in the horizontal plane.
source: Interaural time differences (ITDs) are used by many species to localize sounds in the horizontal plane.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: In mammals, neurons in the medial superior olive (MSO) are sensitive to both ITD and sound frequency.
source: In mammals, neurons in the medial superior olive (MSO), just three synapses away from the cochlear receptors, are sensitive to both ITD and sound frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: MSO neurons are just three synapses away from the cochlear receptors.
source: In mammals, neurons in the medial superior olive (MSO), just three synapses away from the cochlear receptors, are sensitive to both ITD and sound frequency.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge of the auditory pathway.

claim: MSO neurons project to neurons in the inferior colliculus (IC), which inherit ITD and frequency sensitivity properties.
source: They project to neurons in the inferior colliculus (IC), which inherit these properties.
evidence: This is established knowledge of auditory pathway connectivity and functional properties.

claim: For a 600 Hz tone, the neuron shown in Figure 1A responds maximally at a 'best ITD' of 345 μs.
source: For a 600 Hz tone, the neuron shown in Figure 1A, recorded in the IC of a cat, responds maximally at a 'best ITD' of 345 μs, close to the maximum natural ITD reported for cat (about 350 μs) (Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: The maximum natural ITD reported for cat is about 350 μs.
source: For a 600 Hz tone, the neuron shown in Figure 1A, recorded in the IC of a cat, responds maximally at a 'best ITD' of 345 μs, close to the maximum natural ITD reported for cat (about 350 μs) (Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roth et al., 1980.

claim: In the Jeffress model, ITD tuning arises from the detection of coincidences between spikes relayed from auditory nerve fibers tuned to the same frequency at the two ears.
source: In the Jeffress model, the textbook model of ITD processing (Jeffress, 1948; Joris and Yin, 2007), ITD tuning arises from the detection of coincidences between spikes relayed from auditory nerve fibers tuned to the same frequency at the two ears, and the neuron responds maximally when the sound's ITD equals the mismatch in axonal conduction delay between inputs from the two cochleae.
evidence: This is a description of the Jeffress model supported by citations.

claim: The Jeffress model predicts that, for a given neuron, ITD tuning is independent of the sound's frequency.
source: This model predicts that, for a given neuron, ITD tuning is independent of the sound's frequency.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the Jeffress model as described.

claim: At 900 Hz, the neuron of Figure 1 is tuned to an ITD of 158 μs.
source: However, at 900 Hz, the neuron of Figure 1 is tuned to an ITD of 158 μs and barely responds to an ITD of 345 μs, while at 400 Hz the neuron responds maximally at 500 μs and is much less responsive at 345 μs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: At 400 Hz, the neuron of Figure 1 responds maximally at 500 μs.
source: However, at 900 Hz, the neuron of Figure 1 is tuned to an ITD of 158 μs and barely responds to an ITD of 345 μs, while at 400 Hz the neuron responds maximally at 500 μs and is much less responsive at 345 μs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: The range of best ITDs that the neuron in Figure 1 shows at different stimulus frequencies spans several hundred μs.
source: In fact, the range of best ITDs that this neuron shows at different stimulus frequencies spans several hundred μs (Figure 1B), which is large considering that the maximum natural ITD in cats is ∼350 μs.
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1B and stated in the text.

claim: The ITD tuning of binaural neurons varies broadly with sound frequency.
source: Thus, the ITD tuning of this neuron varies broadly with sound frequency.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of cats.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yin and Kuwada, 1983.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of guinea pigs.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McAlpine et al., 1996 and Palmer and Kuwada, 2005.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of rabbits.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwada et al., 1987.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of chinchilla.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bremen and Joris, 2013.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of gerbils.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Day and Semple, 2011.

claim: Frequency-dependent ITD tuning has been observed in binaural neurons of dogs.
source: This property has been observed in binaural neurons of many species, including cats (Yin and Kuwada, 1983), guinea pigs (McAlpine et al., 1996; Palmer and Kuwada, 2005), rabbits (Kuwada et al., 1987), chinchilla (Bremen and Joris, 2013), gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) and dogs (Goldberg and Brown, 1969), but no functional significance has been associated with it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg and Brown, 1969.

claim: Neurons tuned to low frequencies tend to have larger best ITDs than high-frequency neurons.
source: Readers should note that this property is observed within neurons as a function of frequency, and differs from the population property that has also been widely observed, where neurons tuned to low frequencies tend to have larger best ITDs than high-frequency neurons (McAlpine et al., 1996; Hancock and Delgutte, 2004; Joris et al., 2006; Day and Semple, 2011; Bremen and Joris, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The acoustic ITD varies with frequency for a given source position due to sound diffraction by the head.
source: On the other hand, it is known that in natural environments, the acoustic ITD itself varies not only with spatial position but also with frequency, due to sound diffraction by the head (Roth et al., 1980) and early reflections from the ground (Gourévitch and Brette, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the acoustical measurements presented.

claim: The acoustic ITD varies with frequency due to early reflections from the ground.
source: On the other hand, it is known that in natural environments, the acoustic ITD itself varies not only with spatial position but also with frequency, due to sound diffraction by the head (Roth et al., 1980) and early reflections from the ground (Gourévitch and Brette, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gourévitch and Brette, 2012 and the acoustical measurements presented.

claim: The variation of ITD with frequency can be substantial at the scale of a single neuron's receptive field.
source: Here we show with acoustical recordings and simulations that the variation of ITD with frequency can be substantial at the scale of a single neuron's receptive field.
evidence: This is supported by the acoustical analyses presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: The detailed statistics of ITD variation with frequency are matched by the tuning of binaural neurons.
source: We then show that the detailed statistics of this variation are matched by the tuning of binaural neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Slight mismatches in the frequency tuning of auditory nerve fibers projecting to binaural neurons are a plausible mechanism to explain tuning to complex binaural features.
source: Finally, we show that slight mismatches in the frequency tuning of auditory nerve fibers projecting to binaural neurons are a plausible mechanism to explain tuning to complex binaural features of ecological environments, and we show the existence of asymmetries in the spectral properties of MSO inputs using intracellular recordings.
evidence: This is supported by the coincidence analysis in Figure 6 and intracellular recordings in Figure 7.

claim: Asymmetries exist in the spectral properties of MSO inputs.
source: Finally, we show that slight mismatches in the frequency tuning of auditory nerve fibers projecting to binaural neurons are a plausible mechanism to explain tuning to complex binaural features of ecological environments, and we show the existence of asymmetries in the spectral properties of MSO inputs using intracellular recordings.
evidence: This is supported by the intracellular recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: 186 IC neurons of cats were examined with characteristic frequencies between 100 and 3300 Hz.
source: We examined ITD tuning in 186 IC neurons of cats tuned at a characteristic frequency (CF, frequency of lowest rate threshold) between 100 and 3300 Hz (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed in the study.

claim: The best ITDs of a neuron at different frequencies span on average a range of 128 μs (± 240 μs).
source: We found that the best ITDs of a neuron, at the different frequencies to which they were sensitive, spanned on average a range of 128 μs (± 240 μs) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cats can discriminate ITDs differing by only 20 μs.
source: This extent is large, considering the maximum natural ITD reported for cats (∼350 μs) and their ability to discriminate ITDs differing by only 20 μs (Wakeford and Robinson, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wakeford and Robinson, 1974.

claim: Best phase (BP) is defined as best ITD × frequency.
source: The best ITD can be expressed relative to the period of the tone's frequency f, and is then called the best phase (BP): BP = best ITD × f (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: For a neuron with a fixed best ITD that does not depend on frequency, BP is a linear function of frequency with 0 y-intercept.
source: For a neuron with a fixed best ITD that does not depend on frequency, BP is a linear function of frequency with 0 y-intercept.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the definition of BP.

claim: Characteristic phase (CP) is the offset at 0 Hz in the linear fit of BP vs frequency.
source: But the neuron shown in Figure 1D does not fit this simple relationship: a better fit is a linear relationship with an offset at 0 Hz, called the characteristic phase (CP), measured between −0.5 and 0.5 cycle.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Characteristic delay (CD) is the slope of the linear regression of BP vs frequency.
source: The slopes of linear regressions are called characteristic delays (CD; Figure 1D,F) (Yin and Kuwada, 1983).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript, supported by citation, and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: CP is broadly distributed across an entire cycle.
source: We found that CP was broadly distributed across an entire cycle (Figure 1E), indicating that the best ITD of many neurons is not fixed but depends on frequency.
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1E.

claim: CDs are mainly positive and mostly within the natural range of 350 μs.
source: In our neurons, the CDs are mainly positive (corresponding to contralateral leading sounds) and mostly within the natural range of 350 μs, but a minority of cells have negative CDs (38%) and a smaller minority have CDs larger than 350 μs (19%, grey area in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 38% of cells have negative CDs.
source: In our neurons, the CDs are mainly positive (corresponding to contralateral leading sounds) and mostly within the natural range of 350 μs, but a minority of cells have negative CDs (38%) and a smaller minority have CDs larger than 350 μs (19%, grey area in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 19% of cells have CDs larger than 350 μs.
source: In our neurons, the CDs are mainly positive (corresponding to contralateral leading sounds) and mostly within the natural range of 350 μs, but a minority of cells have negative CDs (38%) and a smaller minority have CDs larger than 350 μs (19%, grey area in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CDs are negatively correlated with CPs.
source: Most intriguingly, CDs are negatively correlated with CPs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1G and confirmed by statistical analysis.

claim: The negative correlation between CP and CD is not due to measurement artifacts.
source: We checked with bootstrap analysis that this negative correlation is not due to measurement artifacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The acoustic ITD varies with frequency due to sound diffraction by head and body.
source: It is known that the acoustic ITD itself varies not only with spatial position but also with frequency, due to sound diffraction by head and body (Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the acoustical measurements presented.

claim: The patterns of ITD variation with frequency are consistent with previous acoustical measurements in cats using tones.
source: These patterns are consistent with previous acoustical measurements in cats using tones (Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roth et al., 1980.

claim: The global structure of ITD vs frequency patterns is consistent with a spherical model of the head.
source: The global structure of these patterns is consistent with a spherical model of the head (Kuhn, 1977) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuhn, 1977 and comparison with Figure 2E.

claim: The fine structure of ITD vs frequency patterns depends on posture.
source: However, their fine structure depends on posture (Figure 2C,D, cat's head in a different position), on the presence of a ground (Figure 2E,F, spherical head model without and with a ground plane), and on whether the source is in the front or in the back (Figure 2A–D, solid vs dashed curves)—because of reflections on the body of the cat.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing different conditions in Figure 2.

claim: The fine structure of ITD vs frequency patterns depends on the presence of a ground.
source: However, their fine structure depends on posture (Figure 2C,D, cat's head in a different position), on the presence of a ground (Figure 2E,F, spherical head model without and with a ground plane), and on whether the source is in the front or in the back (Figure 2A–D, solid vs dashed curves)—because of reflections on the body of the cat.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing conditions with and without ground in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The fine structure of ITD vs frequency patterns depends on whether the source is in the front or in the back.
source: However, their fine structure depends on posture (Figure 2C,D, cat's head in a different position), on the presence of a ground (Figure 2E,F, spherical head model without and with a ground plane), and on whether the source is in the front or in the back (Figure 2A–D, solid vs dashed curves)—because of reflections on the body of the cat.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing solid vs dashed curves in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Reflections on the ground or on the body of the cat come too early to be separated from the direct signal.
source: We remark that reflections on the ground or on the body of the cat come too early to be separated from the direct signal (Gourévitch and Brette, 2012) and they must be considered as an integral part of the binaural signal received by the animal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gourévitch and Brette, 2012 and physical reasoning about reflection delays.

claim: In ecological conditions, the ITD generally varies with frequency for a given source position.
source: Thus in ecological conditions, the ITD generally varies with frequency for a given source position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the acoustical measurements and simulations presented.

claim: Natural signals typically have a certain bandwidth.
source: Natural signals do not consist of a single frequency but typically have a certain bandwidth, and individual binaural neurons integrate signal information from a range of frequencies, which matches the bandwidth of filtering in the cochlea (Mc Laughlin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is general knowledge about natural sounds and auditory processing, supported by citation.

claim: Individual binaural neurons integrate signal information from a range of frequencies that matches the bandwidth of filtering in the cochlea.
source: Natural signals do not consist of a single frequency but typically have a certain bandwidth, and individual binaural neurons integrate signal information from a range of frequencies, which matches the bandwidth of filtering in the cochlea (Mc Laughlin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mc Laughlin et al., 2007.

claim: If a neuron were tuned to a fixed ITD, it would be most responsive to different azimuths at different frequencies.
source: If a neuron were tuned to a fixed ITD (e.g., 325 μs, in Figure 3B, top), then it would be most responsive to different azimuths at different frequencies.
evidence: This is a logical inference illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: If a neuron were tuned to a fixed spatial azimuth, its best ITD would vary with frequency to match the variation of ITD with frequency at that position.
source: On the other hand, if the neuron were tuned to a fixed spatial azimuth, then its best ITD would vary with frequency to match the variation of ITD with frequency at that position (Figure 3B, bottom).
evidence: This is a logical inference illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The relationship between ITD and frequency is not fixed but depends on variables in listener, source, and environment.
source: Since the relationship between ITD and frequency is not fixed but depends on variables in listener, source, and environment—as illustrated in Figure 2—we looked for statistical correspondences between acoustical and neural measurements.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the variations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The acoustic measurements show a unimodal and broad CP distribution with a small but significant positive bias.
source: In agreement with the physiological data, the acoustic measurements show a unimodal and broad CP distribution, with a small but significant positive bias (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 4A.

claim: The acoustic CDs are mainly positive and mostly within 350 μs, but with a sizeable number of data points with negative or with large CDs.
source: Consistent with the measured neurons, the acoustic CDs are mainly positive and mostly within 350 μs, but with a sizeable number of data points with negative or with large CDs (Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 for negative CDs).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The acoustic data show an inverse correlation between CD and CP.
source: Finally, the acoustic data also show an inverse correlation between CD and CP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 4C.

claim: Key properties of neural CD and CP are well-matched to binaural acoustics.
source: Thus, key properties of neural CD and CP, which are the main metrics that have been used in the description of tuning to ITD, are well-matched to binaural acoustics studied with these same metrics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of neural and acoustical data in Figure 4.

claim: The distribution of neural CDs and CPs and acoustical CDs and CPs are similarly constrained.
source: First, we provide evidence that the distribution of neural CDs and CPs and acoustical CDs and CPs are similarly constrained.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Large CDs are present acoustically.
source: Second, large CDs are present acoustically.
evidence: This is observable in Figure 4B.

claim: The binaural tuning of IC cells is constrained by the range of delays that the animal experiences.
source: Taken together our results suggest that the binaural tuning of IC cells is constrained by the range of delays that the animal experiences.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the match between neural and acoustical data.

claim: Non-zero CPs in the neural data have puzzled investigators since the first reports of ITD-sensitivity.
source: Non-zero CPs in the neural data have puzzled investigators since the first reports of ITD-sensitivity, both in terms of their physiological origin and their functional significance (Rose et al., 1966; Yin and Kuwada, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: There has been a discrepancy between the distribution of physiological CDs and acoustical phase ITDs.
source: Perhaps even more puzzling has been the discrepancy observed between the distribution of physiological CDs and acoustical (phase) ITDs, for example, as reported in HRTF measurements (for cat: [Roth et al., 1980; Tollin and Koka, 2009], and Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Neuronal CDs seem to cover an 'unnecessarily' wide range including ITDs that animals will not naturally encounter.
source: As was pointed out since the first physiological data became available (McFadden, 1973), neuronal CDs seem to cover an 'unnecessarily' wide range including ITDs that animals will not naturally encounter.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McFadden, 1973.

claim: The appropriate comparison is between physiological CDs and acoustical CDs (envelope ITDs), not phase ITDs.
source: However, the appropriate comparison is not between physiological CDs and acoustical phase ITDs, but with acoustical CDs (i.e., envelope ITDs).
evidence: This is a key interpretive insight of the manuscript.

claim: Due to the frequency dependence of the phase ITD, acoustical CDs have a wide distribution and actually exceed the range of physiological CDs.
source: As shown here for acoustical measurements (Figure 4B), due to the frequency dependence of the phase ITD, CDs have a wide distribution and actually exceed the range of physiological CDs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The range of acoustical CDs that drives a given cell can exceed the range of phase ITDs computed from HRTF data.
source: The range of acoustical CDs that drives a given cell can therefore exceed the range of phase ITDs computed from HRTF data.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the frequency-dependence of ITD.

claim: The frequency-dependence of ITD should apply to other species because it reflects the physical interaction of sound with the ears, head, body, and ground plane.
source: Because the frequency-dependence of ITD reported here reflects the physical interaction of the sound with the ears, head, body, and ground plane, it should also apply to other species.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the physical nature of the phenomenon.

claim: In humans, ITDs dominate below approximately 1.5 kHz.
source: We applied our analysis to HRTFs of humans (Figure 8A–C), for whom ITDs dominate below ∼1.5 kHz (Wightman and Kistler, 1992; Macpherson and Middlebrooks, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wightman and Kistler, 1992 and Macpherson and Middlebrooks, 2002.

claim: The same basic relationship between acoustical CD and CP is present in human HRTFs.
source: The same basic relationship between acoustical CD and CP is present.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: The binaural cues that an auditory system has to process in ecological environments are much more complex and rich than in idealized settings.
source: Our study emphasizes the notion that the binaural cues that an auditory system has to process in ecological environments are much more complex and rich than in idealized settings.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Sound diffraction by the head and body is always present, even in anechoic environments.
source: We have focused here on the contribution of sound diffraction by the head and body, a phenomenon that is always present, even in anechoic environments.
evidence: This is a statement about the physics of sound diffraction.

claim: The effect of sound diffraction depends on the detailed morphology of the animal and varies with posture in a systematic way.
source: Because the effect depends on the detailed morphology of the animal, it varies with posture in a systematic way (see Figure 2C,D and [Rébillat et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C,D and supported by citation.

claim: Early reflections from the ground produce interferences with the direct sound that result in large frequency-dependent variations of ITD, especially at low frequencies.
source: Early reflections, in particular from the ground (again a constant element in ecological environments of terrestrial animals), produce interferences with the direct sound that result in large frequency-dependent variations of ITD, especially at low frequencies (Gourévitch and Brette, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gourévitch and Brette, 2012 and demonstrated in Figure 2F and Figure 5.

claim: Ground reflections typically arrive very shortly after the direct sound and are therefore an integral part of the binaural signal received by the animal.
source: Ground reflections typically arrive very shortly after the direct sound and are therefore an integral part of the binaural signal received by the animal.
evidence: This is based on physical reasoning about reflection delays.

claim: The interferences produced by ground reflections are determined primarily by the delay of the reflection and secondarily by the nature of the reflecting object.
source: The interferences they produce are determined primarily by the delay of the reflection (related to the distance) and secondarily by the nature of the reflecting object (grass, sand, snow, etc).
evidence: This is based on physical reasoning about acoustic reflections.

claim: Many natural sound sources are large and directional, not point sources producing spherical wavefronts.
source: For example, natural sound sources are rarely point sources producing spherical wavefronts, as assumed in most studies. Many are large (a river) and directional (human speech), some are partially occluded by objects (a prey hiding in a bush).
evidence: This is general knowledge about natural sound sources.

claim: The sound of one's own footstep travels through air but also through the body, which produces different acoustical cues.
source: The sound of one's own footstep travels through air but also through the body, which produces different acoustical cues (Hood, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hood, 1962.

claim: The binaural system of animals is adapted to complex natural acoustical cues.
source: We suggest that the binaural system of animals is adapted to these complex natural acoustical cues.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: If ITD depends on the position of the pinnae or posture, then proprioceptive information must be taken into account to interpret binaural cues.
source: For example, if ITD depends on the position of the pinnae, or posture, as is the case for the cat (Figure 2, and [Tollin and Koka, 2009]), then proprioceptive information must be taken into account to interpret binaural cues.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the dependence of ITD on posture.

claim: The fact that ITD depends on factors other than azimuthal position implies that binaural neurons in the MSO are not tuned to source direction per se, but rather to temporal binaural features of acoustical spaces.
source: The fact that ITD depends on factors other than azimuthal position implies that binaural neurons in the MSO are not tuned to source direction per se, but rather to temporal binaural features of acoustical spaces—a notion that generalizes frequency-independent ITD.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the complexity of ITD cues.

claim: If binaural tuning develops from exposure to natural sounds, then it would be expected that its properties reflect those of ecological acoustical environments.
source: If binaural tuning develops from exposure to natural sounds (Seidl and Grothe, 2005), then it would be expected that its properties reflect those of ecological acoustical environments, especially given that very small cochlear disparities give rise to significant frequency-dependence of ITD tuning in binaural neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citation and the data in Figure 6.

claim: Very small cochlear disparities give rise to significant frequency-dependence of ITD tuning in binaural neurons.
source: If binaural tuning develops from exposure to natural sounds (Seidl and Grothe, 2005), then it would be expected that its properties reflect those of ecological acoustical environments, especially given that very small cochlear disparities give rise to significant frequency-dependence of ITD tuning in binaural neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: CF mismatches can generate nonlinear phase-frequency relationships (CP ≠ 0).
source: In previous work, nonlinear phase-frequency relationships (i.e., where the best ITD is not constant) are typically considered to be 'biological noise'. Thus, even though frequency-dependent best ITDs are clearly an important characteristic of the physiological data (Figure 1), there are to our knowledge no functional interpretations of this characteristic. The observation (Figure 6) that CF mismatches can generate nonlinear phase-frequency relationships (CP ≠ 0), combined with the presence of such relationships in the binaural and acoustic data, suggest a rather simple new view on neural binaural properties.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Limitations in the accuracy of wiring in the binaural system produce a property that benefits binaural hearing.
source: The view is that limitations in the accuracy of wiring in the binaural system produce a property that benefits binaural hearing.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Refinements of wiring in combination with mismatches in axonal delays produce a range of binaural sensitivities well-matched to the acoustic scenes that the system is faced with.
source: Refinements of this wiring in combination with mismatches in axonal delays produce a range of binaural sensitivities well-matched to the acoustic scenes that the system is faced with.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Random CF mismatches in the wiring to the contralateral and ipsilateral pathways to IC could account for the negative correlation between CF and range of best ITDs measured with delayed noise.
source: It was previously shown that random CF mismatches in the wiring to the contralateral and ipsilateral pathways to IC could account for the negative correlation between CF and range of best ITDs measured with delayed noise (Joris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Joris et al., 2006.

claim: Appropriate CF and axonal delay mismatches can account for the dependence of best ITD on tone frequency within single cells, matching acoustical properties.
source: Here we show that appropriate CF and axonal delay mismatches can account for the dependence of best ITD on tone frequency within single cells, matching acoustical properties.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling and data analysis presented.

claim: Various mechanisms have been proposed to account for the best delays of ITD-sensitive neurons, including axonal length.
source: Besides cochlear disparities, a range of mechanisms have been proposed to account for the best delays of ITD-sensitive neurons: axonal length (Jeffress, 1948), phase-locked inhibition (Brand et al., 2002), asymmetric placement of the axon (Zhou et al., 2005), asymmetry in synaptic kinetics between contra- and ipsilateral inputs (Jercog et al., 2010), differences in axonal conduction time (Seidl et al., 2010), and phase delays generated by the interaction of intrinsic properties with input spike patterns (Franken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a review of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is unclear which mechanism or mix of mechanisms accounts for ITD tuning, or whether the main mechanism has not been identified yet.
source: All of these proposals face difficulties to explain all the data available, and it is at present unclear which of these mechanisms, or perhaps mix of mechanisms, is in place, or whether perhaps the main mechanism has not been identified yet.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: Axonal length and conduction time are expected to generate pure time delays and would not generate CPs different from 0.
source: Axonal length and conduction time are expected to generate pure time delays and would therefore not generate CPs different from 0.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of these mechanisms.

claim: The original proposal of phase-locked inhibition predicted that best ITD at different frequencies was little affected by stimulus frequency (CP = 0).
source: The report first proposing phase-locked inhibition as a source of internal delay (Brand et al., 2002) provided model results illustrating how best ITD at different frequencies was little affected by stimulus frequency, that is, also predicted that inhibition would be equivalent to a pure time delay (CP = 0).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brand et al., 2002.

claim: More extensive modeling showed that adjustment of inhibitory parameters allows creation of a wide range of non-zero CP values, but CP remained within 0.1 cycle when more realistic inhibitory synaptic time constants were used.
source: Later, more extensive modeling (Day and Semple, 2011) showed that adjustment of model inhibitory parameters allows creation of a wide range of non-zero CP values, but that CP remained within 0.1 cycle when more realistic inhibitory synaptic time constants were used.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Day and Semple, 2011.

claim: Asymmetrical axonal placement, asymmetry in synaptic kinetics, and phase-locked inhibition received little experimental support from a recent in vivo intracellular MSO study.
source: However, these two proposals, as well as phase-locked inhibition, received little experimental support from a recent in vivo intracellular MSO study (Franken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Franken et al., 2015.

claim: Cochlear disparities have been proposed as a mechanism for generating internal delays, in place of axonal delay mismatches.
source: Cochlear disparities have been proposed before as a mechanism for generating internal delays, in place of axonal delay mismatches (Schroeder, 1977; Shamma et al., 1989; Bonham and Lewis, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schroeder, 1977; Shamma et al., 1989; Bonham and Lewis, 1999.

claim: The original form of the cochlear disparity hypothesis, where such disparities are the sole source of internal delays, has been rejected in the barn owl.
source: The original form of that hypothesis, where such disparities are the sole source of internal delays, has been rejected in the barn owl: CF mismatches are observed but they are relatively small and do not correlate with ITD tuning (Pena et al., 2001; Fischer and Peña, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pena et al., 2001 and Fischer and Peña, 2009.

claim: In the barn owl, CF mismatches are significant as they contribute predicted delays of up to 50 μs.
source: They are nonetheless significant as they contribute predicted delays of up to 50 μs (Pena et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pena et al., 2001.

claim: The proposed mechanism combines small CF mismatches and axonal delay mismatches.
source: Importantly, in contrast with the original cochlear disparity hypothesis, our proposed mechanism combines small CF mismatches (just 40 Hz in Figure 6) and axonal delay mismatches.
evidence: This is the mechanism proposed in the manuscript.

claim: A mix of cochlear disparities and pure time delays was proposed to account for non-linear phase-frequency relationships observed in gerbil MSO responses.
source: A mix of cochlear disparities and pure time delays was also proposed to account for non-linear phase-frequency relationships observed in gerbil MSO responses (Day and Semple, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Day and Semple, 2011.

claim: In cat MSO, monaural best frequencies differed by 0.2 octaves or less for 13 of 18 cells.
source: In cat MSO, (Yin and Chan, 1990) reported that monaural best frequencies differed by 0.2 octaves or less for 13 of the 18 cells (and more for 5 cells).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yin and Chan, 1990.

claim: CF mismatches of 0.2 octaves or less are sufficient to produce the observed frequency-dependence of best ITD.
source: As we show in Figure 6, this order of magnitude is sufficient to produce the observed frequency-dependence of best ITD.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Intracellular recordings from MSO neurons confirm that monaural inputs can differ in spectral properties.
source: Intracellular recordings from MSO neurons allowed us to directly measure the monaural inputs and confirm that they can differ in spectral properties.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 7.

claim: The data are from the IC, one synapse removed from the sites of binaural interaction.
source: Our data are from the IC, one synapse removed from the sites of binaural interaction.
evidence: This is a statement about the recording site.

claim: Frequency-dependent properties of ITD tuning observed in IC neurons are inherited from the MSO.
source: In our mechanistic explanation, we have assumed that frequency-dependent properties of ITD tuning observed in IC neurons are inherited from the MSO.
evidence: This is an assumption stated in the manuscript.

claim: Electrophysiological data in the MSO of cats and gerbils show frequency-dependent ITD tuning (broad distributions of CP).
source: This is in agreement with electrophysiological data in the MSO of cats (Yin and Chan, 1990) and gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011; van der Heijden et al., 2013), which also show frequency-dependent ITD tuning (broad distributions of CP).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yin and Chan, 1990; Day and Semple, 2011; van der Heijden et al., 2013.

claim: Nonlinearities at the level of the IC could reflect convergence of inputs from binaural neurons in MSO, LSO, and DNLL.
source: Alternatively, nonlinearities at the level of the IC could reflect convergence of inputs, for example, from binaural neurons in MSO, LSO, and DNLL (McAlpine et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: LSO neurons have CP close to 0.5.
source: For example, LSO neurons have CP close to 0.5 (Joris, 1996; Tollin and Yin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joris, 1996 and Tollin and Yin, 2005.

claim: Neurons with CP close to 0 have been categorized as 'peakers', because peaks of their ITD selectivity curves align across frequency.
source: Neurons with CP close to 0 have been categorized as 'peakers', because peaks of their ITD selectivity curves align across frequency, while neurons with CP close to 0.5 have been categorized as 'troughers', because troughs align across frequency (Batra et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of a categorization scheme supported by citation.

claim: Neurons with CP close to 0.5 have been categorized as 'troughers', because troughs of their ITD selectivity curves align across frequency.
source: Neurons with CP close to 0 have been categorized as 'peakers', because peaks of their ITD selectivity curves align across frequency, while neurons with CP close to 0.5 have been categorized as 'troughers', because troughs align across frequency (Batra et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of a categorization scheme supported by citation.

claim: Neurons with intermediate CP are categorized as 'tweeners', presumably reflecting a combination of MSO and LSO inputs.
source: Neurons with intermediate CP are then categorized as 'tweeners', presumably reflecting a combination of MSO and LSO inputs.
evidence: This is a description of a categorization scheme.

claim: The electrophysiological data showed no clear categories in the distribution of CP.
source: However, our electrophysiological data showed no clear categories in the distribution of CP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is observable in Figure 1E.

claim: The distribution of CP was broad and unimodal around CP = 0, which argues against the categorization of cells as peaker, trougher, and tweener.
source: Instead, the distribution was broad and unimodal around CP = 0, which argues against the categorization of cells as peaker, trougher, and tweener.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 1E.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in the MSO of cats and gerbils show cells with non-zero CP.
source: In addition, electrophysiological studies in the MSO of cats (Yin and Chan, 1990) and gerbils (Day and Semple, 2011) also show cells with non-zero CP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yin and Chan, 1990 and Day and Semple, 2011.

claim: Very small mismatches in CF of inputs to binaural cells are sufficient to produce significantly non-zero CP, without postulating any additional mechanism than coincidence detection.
source: Our auditory nerve data shows that very small mismatches in CF of inputs to binaural cells are sufficient to produce significantly non-zero CP, without postulating any additional mechanism than coincidence detection (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: One attractive feature of cochlear disparities is that they provide a simple mechanism to generate non-zero CPs when combined with a physiological source of pure time delays.
source: In summary, while the mechanisms of ITD tuning remain unclear, one attractive feature of cochlear disparities is that they provide a simple mechanism to generate non-zero CPs, which we show here are a likely desirable property of the binaural system as they match the acoustics that animals face, when combined with a physiological source of pure time delays.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the mechanistic discussion.
